Nose & Paranasal Sinuses

Lecture 10 · Part 1The External Nose & Nasal Cavity

Lecturer: Dr Nur Hassan, BDS, PGT (Oral Surg), PhD — Senior Lecturer, CSU.

External nose

Bones & landmarks

  • Two nasal bones
  • Nasion and glabella
  • Naris (nostril)

Cartilages

  • Lateral nasal cartilage
  • Alar cartilages (multiple)
  • Septal cartilage

There are recognised racial variations in the nasal bone angle and the width of the nose.

Apertures

AperturePosition
Piriform (anterior nasal) apertureAnterior — seen on the anterior view of the skull
ChoanaePosterior — bounded by the horizontal plate of the palatine bone and the palatine process of the maxilla

Nasal septum

  • Partly bony: the vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid
  • Partly cartilaginous: the septal cartilage

Boundaries of the nasal cavity

BoundaryFormed by
FloorPalatine process of the maxilla and the horizontal plate of the palatine bone
RoofLateral nasal cartilages, nasal bones, nasal processes of the frontal bone, body of the sphenoid, and the body and cribriform plate of the ethmoid
Lateral wallMaxilla, lacrimal bone, ethmoid (superior and middle conchae) and the inferior concha
Note the shared floor: the floor of the nasal cavity is the roof of the mouth. The same two bones form the hard palate — which is why a maxillary lesion can present in either cavity.

Epithelium

EpitheliumLocation
Respiratory epitheliumMiddle and inferior conchae
Olfactory epitheliumSuperior concha — olfactory axons pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb
Why a head injury can cost you your sense of smell: the olfactory axons pass through the delicate cribriform plate. A fracture there shears them, causing anosmia.

Lecture 10 · Part 2The Paranasal Sinuses

The four paired sinuses
MaxillaryFrontalEthmoidSphenoid
  • Reduce the weight of the skull
  • Resonators of the voice
  • Act as shock absorbers in trauma
  • Warm and moisten inhaled air
  • Mucus produced is moved into the nasal cavity by the ciliary action of the columnar cells
  • Drainage into the back of the throat to swallow, or by blowing the nose
Be honest in an exam answer: the lecture itself notes that sinus function is controversial — air conditioning, lightening the skull and speech resonance are proposed roles rather than settled facts.

Lecture 10 · Part 3The Sinuses One by One

Maxillary sinus — the dentist's sinus

FeatureDetail
FloorAlveolar process of the maxilla — 5–10 mm below the nasal floor in adults
RoofFloor of the orbit — the most fragile wall; traversed by the infraorbital nerve
DrainageInto the middle meatus; the opening is on the medial wall, with the sinus lying below the opening
Relationship to teethApices of the 2nd premolar and the 1st and 2nd molars
GrowthTwo periods — before age 3 and between 7 and 18; eruption of the permanent teeth induces growth
NeurovasculatureSmall branches from the facial and maxillary arteries (infraorbital and palatine); innervation is V2
  • Innervated by the PSAN, MSAN and ASAN — all from V2
  • The ostium lies in the centre of the hiatus semilunaris, within the middle meatus
  • Lymphatic drainage: submandibular lymph nodes
The clinical crux: the ostium sits high on the medial wall, above the floor of the sinus. Drainage therefore works against gravity when upright, which is a large part of why the maxillary sinus is so prone to infection.
Why sinusitis mimics toothache: the roots of the upper posterior teeth sit right against the sinus floor and share V2 innervation — so sinus inflammation can present as pain in several upper teeth at once, with none of them being the culprit.

Ethmoid sinuses (air cells)

  • Roof: frontal bone anteriorly; sphenoid and palatine posteriorly
  • Opening: anterior and middle cells → middle meatus; posterior cells → superior meatus
  • Growth: a few cells present at birth; 6–10 cells in adulthood
  • Many variations in shape
  • Neurovasculature: anterior and middle cells from the anterior ethmoidal, posterior from the posterior ethmoidal branches of the ophthalmic artery; innervation V1 (anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves)

Frontal sinuses

  • The most variable of all the sinuses — one or both are absent in 5% of the population
  • Floor: roof of the orbit
  • Opening: anterior part of the middle meatus, via the frontonasal duct
  • Growth: appear late — not seen on images until age 6
  • Neurovasculature: arteries and veins from ophthalmic branches; innervation V1 (supraorbital branch)
A serious caveat from the slide: venous blood from the frontal sinus reaches the intracranial venous sinuses — so frontal sinusitis carries a risk of intracranial spread.

Sphenoid sinuses

  • Variable and often asymmetric
  • Opening: into the sphenoethmoidal recess, superior to the superior concha — the opening lies 10–20 mm above the sinus floor
  • Relationships: pituitary gland, optic nerves, internal carotid arteries and the cavernous sinuses — infection here can be dangerous
  • Growth: develops during mid childhood, complete at age 12–15
  • Neurovasculature: from the posterior ethmoidal branch of the ophthalmic artery; innervation V1
Likely copy-paste error on this slide: it gives the floor of the sphenoid sinus as “roof of the orbit”. That describes the frontal sinus, on the previous slide. The sphenoid sinus sits in the body of the sphenoid, with the pituitary gland in the sella turcica above it — which is exactly why it is the surgical route used for pituitary surgery.
Trans-sphenoidal surgery: because the pituitary sits directly above the sphenoid sinus, surgeons reach pituitary tumours through the nose and the sphenoid sinus rather than opening the skull.

Lecture 10 · Part 4Drainage & the Osteomeatal Complex

Osteomeatal complex

  • The site of drainage of the maxillary, frontal, and anterior and middle ethmoidal sinuses
  • Comprises the ethmoidal bulla, hiatus semilunaris and uncinate process
  • It is the final common pathway for drainage and ventilation of the frontal and maxillary sinuses and the anterior ethmoidal cells
  • Inflammation can block it, causing sinus infection, facial pain and headache
Why this small area matters so much: because three sinus groups all drain through one narrow channel, a little swelling there blocks all of them at once. That is the anatomical rationale behind functional endoscopic sinus surgery.

Where each sinus drains

Drains intoStructures
Superior meatusPosterior ethmoidal air cells
Sphenoethmoidal recessSphenoid sinus — superior to the superior concha
Middle meatusFrontal, maxillary, and middle and anterior ethmoidal sinuses
Inferior meatusThe nasolacrimal duct — not a sinus
The one to memorise: the inferior meatus takes no sinus at all — only the nasolacrimal duct. Everything anterior (frontal, maxillary, anterior/middle ethmoid) goes to the middle meatus; posterior ethmoid to the superior meatus; sphenoid to the recess above them all.
Why crying makes your nose run: tears drain through the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus.

Development & imaging

Lecture 10 · Part 5Blood & Nerve Supply

External nose

Supplied mostly by the facial artery, with contributions from branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary arteries.

Nasal septum

Four contributors to the septum
Anterior ethmoidalPosterior ethmoidal Posterior septal branch of sphenopalatineSeptal branch of superior labial

These come from the ophthalmic (anterior and posterior ethmoidal), the maxillary (sphenopalatine, greater palatine) and the facial artery (septal branch of the superior labial).

Kiesselbach’s area (also called Little’s area) is where these vessels anastomose on the anterior septum. It is the site of most anterior nosebleeds, and its rich supply from three different arterial territories is exactly why it bleeds so readily.

Lateral wall & venous drainage

Mostly sphenopalatine branches and the greater palatine artery (both from the maxillary artery), with contributions from the ophthalmic (anterior and posterior ethmoidal) and the facial artery.

Veins accompany the arteries and drain into the facial vein, the ophthalmic veins and the pterygoid venous plexus.

Nerve supply

RegionNerves
Nasal septumMostly the nasopalatine nerve; also the anterior ethmoidal anteriorly
Lateral wallGreater palatine and anterior ethmoidal nerves
Special senseOlfactory nerve (CN I)

General sensation is by trigeminal branches — mostly V1 and V2.

Lecture 10 · Part 6Clinical Correlates

The danger triangle

  • The danger triangle of the face is the area from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, including the nose and maxilla
  • Cause: venous communication via the ophthalmic veins between the facial vein and the cavernous sinus
  • The cavernous sinus lies within the cranial cavity between layers of the meninges, and is a major conduit of venous drainage from the brain

Clinical correlates

ProblemConsequence
SinusitisSinus headache and sinus toothache
Carcinoma of the maxillary sinusMay invade the palate and present as dental pain
Pneumatisation of the sinusRisk of oro-antral communication (OAC) and oro-antral fistula (OAF); affects planning of maxillary implants
Risk of bleedingFrom extra-osseous anastomoses
Surgical accessFunctional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) and endoscopic endonasal skull base surgery
The one you will meet in practice: an oro-antral communication after extracting an upper molar whose roots projected into a pneumatised sinus. Knowing the floor of the sinus sits at the apices of the 2nd premolar and 1st and 2nd molars is what should make you check the radiograph first.
